name: Clear cell sarcoma of soft tissue

clinicalPearls: Rare deep soft-tissue sarcoma of young adults, typically arising in tendons and aponeuroses of the distal extremities, most often around the foot and ankle.
Historically called malignant melanoma of soft parts because of melanocytic differentiation, but it is genetically distinct from cutaneous melanoma.
Defined by a recurrent EWSR1-ATF1 fusion (t(12;22)), with a minority harbouring EWSR1-CREB1; this distinguishes it from melanoma, which lacks these fusions.
Tumour cells express melanocytic markers (S100, HMB-45, Melan-A, SOX10) and contain melanin, so immunohistochemistry alone cannot separate it from metastatic melanoma.
Presents as a slowly enlarging, often painless deep mass attached to tendon or fascia; a long indolent history before diagnosis is characteristic.
Molecular confirmation of the EWSR1 rearrangement (FISH or RT-PCR) is the key diagnostic step when melanoma is in the differential.
Prone to late local recurrence and to lymph-node as well as haematogenous metastasis, with lung the most common distant site.
Wide surgical excision is the mainstay; it responds poorly to conventional cytotoxic chemotherapy and to melanoma immunotherapy regimens.
reference.pathophysiology: Clear cell sarcoma arises from a primitive mesenchymal cell that acquires a balanced chromosomal translocation, most commonly t(12;22)(q13;q12) generating an EWSR1-ATF1 chimeric transcription factor, with a smaller subset carrying EWSR1-CREB1. The fusion protein constitutively activates the microphthalmia-associated transcription factor (MITF) pathway, driving a melanocytic differentiation programme so that the tumour cells synthesise melanin and express melanocyte markers despite a soft-tissue rather than epidermal origin. Aberrant MITF signalling also promotes proliferation and survival. Because the oncogenic driver is a fusion rather than the BRAF/NRAS mutations and high mutational burden seen in cutaneous melanoma, the biology, therapeutic vulnerabilities and immune landscape differ substantially: the tumour has a low mutational load and typically lacks the targetable kinase mutations exploited in melanoma. The cells grow along tendons and aponeuroses in nested and fascicular patterns separated by fibrous septa, correlating with the deep, fascia-anchored masses seen clinically.
additionalDifferentials: Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour with melanocytic features
Cellular blue naevus and other melanocytic proliferations
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the primary site to define soft-tissue extent and relationship to tendon and neurovascular structures
Core needle or open biopsy with expert soft-tissue pathology review
FISH or RT-PCR for EWSR1 rearrangement (EWSR1-ATF1 / EWSR1-CREB1)
Immunohistochemistry panel including S100, HMB-45, Melan-A and SOX10
Contrast CT of the chest to assess for pulmonary metastases
Regional nodal imaging and consideration of sentinel node evaluation given nodal spread
Dermatological and mucosal examination to exclude an occult primary melanoma
redFlags: Rapid enlargement, new pain or skin ulceration over a previously indolent deep mass
Palpable regional lymphadenopathy suggesting nodal metastasis
New respiratory symptoms or pulmonary nodules indicating distant spread
Recurrence at the prior surgical bed after apparently complete excision
Neurological deficit from local invasion of adjacent nerves
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is guarded and strongly linked to tumour size, depth and the presence of nodal or distant metastasis, with large or metastatic tumours carrying poor long-term survival. Late recurrences and metastases occurring many years after treatment are characteristic, so prolonged follow-up is required.
pitfalls: Mislabelling the tumour as metastatic melanoma because of shared melanocytic markers, leading to inappropriate melanoma-directed therapy.
Omitting molecular testing for EWSR1 rearrangement, which is the decisive distinguishing feature.
Underestimating the risk of lymph-node metastasis, which is higher than for most other soft-tissue sarcomas.
Assuming an indolent clinical course means benign disease and delaying definitive wide excision.
Discharging patients from surveillance too early given the propensity for very late relapse.
